Decision — long-running work on the Bus is an operation

Status: accepted 2026-11-03.

Why

Agents spend most of their time waiting: on a build, a merge, a reply from a person. When a Bus request stays open for the whole wait, the caller has to stay alive and connected for it, a broker restart or a lost connection turns the outcome into a guess, and the caller cannot do anything else meanwhile. The Bus broker is deliberately not durable, so the fix is not to make the broker hold the wait. The fix is for the service doing the work to hand back an id at once and keep the outcome itself.

The decision

A service command whose work can outlast a request (minutes rather than seconds) is an operation:

  • Start. The command answers at once with {op}, a string id unique to that service. A caller may supply the id itself so that a retry after a lost reply joins the same work instead of starting it twice.
  • States. An operation is in one of queued, running, done, failed, cancelled, lost or unknown. done, failed, cancelled and lost are terminal and final. unknown means the service has never seen the id; it is not terminal, because a caller may register interest in an id before it submits the work.
  • <svc>.op.done. When an operation reaches a terminal state, the service publishes one <svc>.op.done topic, not retained, carrying {op, state, rc?, log?, reason?} and any service-specific fields. Every terminal state uses this one topic, cancelled included.
  • <svc>.op.get {op}. Answers {op, state, ...} with the same envelope, at any time. A caller that was not listening when op.done went out uses it to catch up.
  • <svc>.op.cancel {op}. Asks for the operation to stop and answers {op, cancelled, state}, where cancelled says whether the request changed anything.
  • Retention. The service keeps a terminal outcome for at least as long as it documents (days, for a build queue), so op.get still answers after the caller has been away.

A caller watches <svc>.op.done and calls <svc>.op.get when it starts waiting and after every reconnect, because op.done is not retained and can be missed. The broker stores nothing for any of this.

Consequences

  • An agent session can register interest in an operation, end its turn and give up its process; the agent supervisor resumes it with the outcome when op.done arrives (see ACP agent sessions on the Bus). The supervisor itself publishes agent.op.done when a session's job ends, so a parent waits on a child the same way.
  • A caller that restarts, or a broker restart, no longer loses an outcome: it is one op.get away.
  • Services adopt this as their long commands are touched. A service whose only long command already has its own status query may answer op.get/op.cancel as aliases over it.

Not doing

  • No durable queue, timers or delivery guarantees in the broker.
  • No generic topic-pattern waits: interest is always in one operation id.
